source.version: Journal version of record: Thinking Skills and Creativity 59 (2026) 101958; received 27 April 2025, revised 14 August 2025, accepted 16 August 2025, available online 18 August 2025 (p. 1)
source.title_on_document: Evaluating AI-assisted creative ideation: A crossover study in higher education

supplement.holds: The document refers to no supplementary material or online appendix. All statistics are in Tables 3 to 9 and the text of Section 4. Data availability: 'Data will be made available on request.' (p. 15)

paper_design_summary: 51 third-year industrial design engineering students at UPC (Spain) were randomly divided into two groups for a two-task crossover in one two-hour session: Group A (n = 24) generated ideas unaided in Task 1 (public transport) and with ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) in Task 2 (university spaces); Group B (n = 27) did the reverse. Each task asked for eight handwritten ideas in 30 minutes. The researchers scored the 728 ideas for fluency, flexibility, originality (unique ideas and solutions), novelty (count of ideas resembling existing products), text elaboration (word count), and image elaboration, and assessed thematic homogenisation (category diversity indices, category sizes, unique contributions) and semantic homogenisation (LaBSE embedding distance to centroid).

studies.label: Randomised crossover experiment, ChatGPT-assisted vs unaided ideation (two tasks, one session)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Order of conditions: AI-assisted (ChatGPT GPT-3.5) first then unaided (Group B), or unaided first then AI-assisted (Group A). Each student did one task in each condition.
assignment.quote: a randomised controlled crossover experiment was employed, in which participants were randomly assigned to one condition for the first task and then switched to the other condition for the second task.
assignment.locator: p. 4, Section 3.2.1; also p. 4-5 'They were then randomly divided into two groups and directed to separate classrooms'; Fig. 1 p. 5

arms.name: AI-assisted
arms.description: Worked in a computer lab with university computers and limited internet access to ChatGPT (GPT-3.5). Group B in Task 1 (27 students, 195 ideas); Group A in Task 2 (24 students, 173 ideas).

arms.name: Unaided
arms.description: Worked in a classroom without computer access or permission to use external resources or electronic devices. Group A in Task 1 (24 students, 158 ideas); Group B in Task 2 (27 students, 202 ideas).

participants.exclusions: No exclusions reported. 51 students were randomly divided into Group A (n = 24, unaided first) and Group B (n = 27, AI first) (Fig. 1); Tables 3-5 report N = 51 with the same group sizes. For the qualitative prompt analysis, 49 of 51 ChatGPT conversations were retrieved (p. 10). Each person appears in both conditions, so Table 4 reports N = 102 person-condition observations.
participants.who: Third-year students of the bachelor's degree in industrial design engineering and product development
participants.quote: The study involved 51 third-year students from the bachelor's degree in industrial design engineering and product development at the Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya - BarcelonaTech (UPC), Spain.
participants.locator: p. 4, Section 3.1; Fig. 1 p. 5; Table 4 note p. 8

ai_tool.how_used: Free use of ChatGPT on lab computers while brainstorming; ideas were written and drawn by hand on pre-printed paper templates, so AI text was not pasted into the deliverable. Students averaged 6.96 prompts per conversation; 48.39 percent of coded prompts were generic requests for ideas (Tables 8-9, p. 12).

task.description: Task 1: generate innovative ideas for improving public transport. Task 2: generate ideas for improving university spaces. Eight ideas per task, each on a separate sheet with space for a drawing and a description.
task.duration: 30 min per task; two-hour session in total

outcomes.name: Originality (count of Unique Ideas and Unique Solutions per participant)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Researchers built an inductive three-level category system (LV1/LV2/LV3) for all 728 ideas, coded blind to condition and identity. Unique Idea = idea in no existing LV3 subcategory; Unique Solution = clearly different solution within an LV3 subcategory. Originality = count of UI and US (Table 2, p. 7; Section 3.2.2, p. 5-6). Analysis: Wilcoxon signed-rank (within person), Mann-Whitney U by task, mixed between-within ANOVA.

contrasts.reported: Unaided 3.27 (1.74) vs AI-assisted 2.94 (1.35); Wilcoxon z = -1.24, p = .216, r = .17; N = 102; Unaided n = 51, AI-assisted n = 51
Group A unaided 2.50 (1.47) vs Group B AI-assisted 3.33 (1.07); U = 437, z = 2.20, p = .028*, r = .31

contrasts.control_arm: Task 2: Group B unaided (n = 27; had used AI in Task 1)
contrasts.reported: Group A AI-assisted 2.50 (1.50) vs Group B unaided 3.96 (1.70); U = 474, z = 2.88, p = .004**, r = .40. Control arm had prior AI exposure in Task 1. Mixed ANOVA: AI usage x condition order interaction Wilks' lambda = 0.747, F(1, 49) = 16.62, p < .001, partial eta^2 = 0.25

outcomes.name: Novelty (count of Existing Solutions per participant; lower = more novel)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of ideas the researchers labelled Existing Solutions (ideas resembling existing products). 'A lower number reflects greater novelty' (Table 2, p. 7). Study-specific metric; the paper notes it needs further validation (p. 14). Sign reversed: a higher printed value means less novel.

contrasts.reported: Existing Solutions count: Unaided 0.55 (0.81) vs AI-assisted 1.00 (0.96); Wilcoxon z = 2.55, p = .011*, r = .36. AI-assisted ideas resembled existing products more often (less novel). Mixed ANOVA main effect of AI usage: Wilks' lambda = 0.872, F(1, 49) = 7.19, p = .010, partial eta^2 = 0.13; condition order F(1, 49) = 1.56, p = .218, partial eta^2 = 0.03
Existing Solutions count: Group A unaided 0.67 (0.87) vs Group B AI-assisted 1.07 (1.07); U = 392, z = 1.36, p = .172, r = .19

contrasts.control_arm: Task 2: Group B unaided (n = 27; had used AI in Task 1)
contrasts.reported: Existing Solutions count: Group A AI-assisted 0.92 (0.83) vs Group B unaided 0.44 (0.75); U = 211, z = -2.35, p = .019*, r = .33

outcomes.name: Flexibility (number of second-level categories explored per participant)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Number of distinct LV2 categories among a participant's ideas (Table 2, p. 7), from the researchers' blind categorisation.

contrasts.reported: Unaided 5.51 (1.78) vs AI-assisted 5.57 (1.36); Wilcoxon z = 0.21, p = .833, r = .03
Group A unaided 4.58 (1.81) vs Group B AI-assisted 5.67 (1.54); U = 440, z = 2.21, p = .027*, r = .31

contrasts.control_arm: Task 2: Group B unaided (n = 27; had used AI in Task 1)
contrasts.reported: Group A AI-assisted 5.46 (1.14) vs Group B unaided 6.33 (1.30); U = 461, z = 2.65, p = .008**, r = .37. Mixed ANOVA AI usage x order interaction: Wilks' lambda = 0.801, F(1, 49) = 12.19, p = .001, partial eta^2 = 0.20

outcomes.name: Fluency (number of ideas generated per participant)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Total number of ideas generated (Table 2, p. 7). Students were asked to produce eight ideas in 30 min (p. 5). The paper says fluency violated ANOVA assumptions and its results 'should be interpreted with caution' (p. 6).

contrasts.reported: Unaided 7.06 (1.54) vs AI-assisted 7.22 (1.08); Wilcoxon z = 0.77, p = .439, r = .11
Group A unaided 6.58 (1.98) vs Group B AI-assisted 7.22 (1.12); U = 374, z = 1.03, p = .304, r = .14

contrasts.control_arm: Task 2: Group B unaided (n = 27; had used AI in Task 1)
contrasts.reported: Group A AI-assisted 7.21 (1.06) vs Group B unaided 7.48 (0.85); U = 373, z = 1.06, p = .289, r = .15

outcomes.name: Text elaboration (word count of the idea description)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Word count of each handwritten idea description (Table 2, p. 7); text extracted by OCR with Gemini and manually verified (p. 7). Not a creativity scoring model; closest listed code. Participant-level mean.

contrasts.reported: Unaided 25.57 (8.06) vs AI-assisted 23.36 (7.66); Wilcoxon z = -2.44, p = .015*, r = .34
Group A unaided 25.54 (8.92) vs Group B AI-assisted 25.19 (7.14); U = 323, z = 0.03, p = .977, r = .00

contrasts.reported: Group A AI-assisted 21.31 (7.85) vs Group B unaided 25.60 (7.39); U = 444, z = 2.26, p = .024*, r = .32

outcomes.name: Image elaboration (representation of human interaction, motion or states, 3D volume)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Three yes/no codes on each idea's drawing: representation of human interaction, of motion or states, of 3D volume (Table 2, p. 7). Coded by the research team (coder identity not stated separately for this metric). The only variable that did not deviate from normality (p. 6).

contrasts.reported: Unaided 1.32 (0.36) vs AI-assisted 1.28 (0.40); Wilcoxon z = -0.18, p = .857, r = .03
Group A unaided 1.35 (0.35) vs Group B AI-assisted 1.20 (0.43); U = 260, z = 1.22, p = .223, r = .17

contrasts.control_arm: Task 2: Group B unaided (n = 27; had used AI in Task 1)
contrasts.reported: Group A AI-assisted 1.36 (0.36) vs Group B unaided 1.29 (0.36); U = 279, z = 0.86, p = .389, r = .12

outcomes.name: Individual-level semantic divergence (spread of each participant's own ideas, LaBSE)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: LaBSE embeddings of OCR'd idea descriptions. Methods: 'average pairwise semantic divergence within each participant's set of ideas' per condition (p. 7); Results: 'average semantic divergence from the centroid per participant' (p. 10). Compares one person's own ideas, so coded flexibility, not diversity; the paper presents it as individual-level homogenisation.

contrasts.reported: Unaided M = 0.28 (SD = 0.03) vs AI-assisted M = 0.29 (SD = 0.03); paired samples t(364) = 3.41, p = .001, d = 0.48, 95 % CI [0.01, 0.03]. Direction coded from printed means (AI divergence higher); the paper's text concludes AI ideas were 'more semantically concentrated'. See open_questions.

outcomes.name: Group-level semantic divergence (cosine distance of each idea to its condition's centroid, LaBSE)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Cosine distance between each idea's LaBSE embedding and the average embedding of its condition (AI-assisted vs unaided), pooled over both tasks and all participants; independent samples t-test across ideas. Higher divergence = more diverse.

contrasts.reported: Unaided M = 0.28 (SD = 0.06) vs AI-assisted M = 0.29 (SD = 0.07); independent samples t(728) = -3.54, p < .001, d = -0.26, 95 % CI [-0.03, -0.01]. Direction coded from printed means and Fig. 3a (AI divergence higher = more diverse); the paper's text reads it as AI ideas 'modestly more semantically similar to the group centroid' (homogenising). See open_questions.
contrasts.locator: p. 10, Section 4.3; Fig. 3a p. 11; idea counts per condition p. 10 (N = 368, N = 360) and Fig. 1 p. 5

diversity_detail.metric: Cosine distance of each idea to the centroid (mean embedding) of its condition
diversity_detail.embedding_model: LaBSE (Language-agnostic BERT Sentence Embedding); text from handwritten sheets via OCR with Gemini, manually verified
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each idea against the centroid of all ideas in its condition (both tasks pooled, all participants)
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Independent samples t-test over idea-level distances (ideas treated as independent; no clustering by participant or task)
diversity_detail.notes: Printed means (0.28 unaided vs 0.29 AI), negative t and d, and Fig. 3a all show higher divergence for AI-assisted ideas, but the abstract and text say semantic divergence was lower with AI. df = 728 equals the total idea count. Centroids are condition-specific and pool two different task prompts.

outcomes.name: Thematic diversity indices (Shannon H' and Simpson 1-D over idea categories)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Shannon and Simpson indices of the distribution of each condition's pooled ideas over LV2 and LV3 categories; also number of LV2/LV3 categories with ideas from each condition. Descriptive only, no test.

contrasts.reported: LV2: categories Unaided 50, AI 51; Shannon 3.538 vs 3.661 (difference -0.123); Simpson 0.964 vs 0.972 (difference -0.008). LV3: categories Unaided 114, AI 117; Shannon 4.503 vs 4.588 (difference -0.085); Simpson 0.990 vs 0.992 (difference -0.002). Paper: comparable diversity, AI 'slightly broader'.

diversity_detail.metric: Shannon index H' and Simpson index 1-D over category frequencies
diversity_detail.computed_over: All ideas of one condition (both tasks, all participants) as one set, at LV2 and LV3
diversity_detail.notes: Table 7 'Difference' row is printed as Unaided minus AI-assisted. Table 6 (p. 9) gives categories exclusive to each condition: LV2 unaided 4, mixed 46, AI 5; LV3 unaided 26, mixed 88, AI 29.

outcomes.name: Category size of ideas (size of the category each idea falls in)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: For each idea, the size of its category; tests whether AI-assisted ideas cluster in larger (dominant) categories. Category level not stated in this passage.

diversity_detail.metric: Mean size of the category containing each idea (larger = more clustered in dominant themes)
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each idea's category membership among all 728 ideas
diversity_detail.notes: Lower category size would mean less clustering; printed AI mean is lower but not significant.

outcomes.name: Unique contributions (Unique Ideas and Unique Solutions) by condition, idea level
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Association between condition and whether an idea is a unique contribution (Unique Idea or Unique Solution, defined relative to the whole 728-idea dataset); chi-square tests on all unique contributions and on UI and US separately. Counts by condition in Table 6.

contrasts.reported: Total unique contributions chi2(1, N = 728) = 2.12, p = .145; Unique Ideas chi2(1, N = 728) = 0.18, p = .670; Unique Solutions chi2(1, N = 728) = 1.56, p = .212. Counts: UI unaided 85 vs AI 81; US unaided 82 vs AI 69; Existing Solutions unaided 28 vs AI 51.

diversity_detail.metric: Share of ideas that are unique contributions (rarity in the pooled dataset)
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each idea classified against all 728 ideas from both conditions
diversity_detail.notes: Overlaps with the participant-level originality count (S1-O1); recorded separately because the paper uses it as a thematic homogenisation test.

outcomes.name: Flexibility in unaided work after AI use (order effect)
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Same metric as S1-O3, on Group B's unaided Task 2 ideas produced after using ChatGPT in Task 1. Comparison is across groups and across tasks (T1 public transport vs T2 university spaces), so task and practice are confounded with prior AI exposure.
outcomes.delay: Same two-hour session; Task 2 started right after the 30-min Task 1

contrasts.treatment_arm: Group B unaided in Task 2, after AI in Task 1 (n = 27)
contrasts.control_arm: Group A unaided in Task 1, no prior AI (n = 24)
contrasts.reported: Group B Task 2 unaided 6.33 (1.30) vs Group A Task 1 unaided 4.58 (1.81) (means from Table 5; no direct test of this pair). Mixed ANOVA AI usage x condition order interaction: Wilks' lambda = 0.801, F(1, 49) = 12.19, p = .001, partial eta^2 = 0.20. Group B higher than Group A across both tasks (Mann-Whitney, Table 5).

outcomes.question: after_ai

outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Same metric as S1-O2 (lower count = more novel), on Group B's unaided Task 2 ideas after AI in Task 1. Cross-group, cross-task comparison.

contrasts.control_arm: Group A unaided in Task 1, no prior AI (n = 24)

sample_overlap.locator: The paper cites Baltà-Salvador et al. (2025, Computer Applications in Engineering Education 33(1), e22817) by the same first author on ChatGPT-assisted ideation (p. 3, p. 13, references p. 15) but does not say whether the two papers share participants.

company_involvement.description: No company involvement stated. 'This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.' Authors declare no competing interests.
company_involvement.locator: p. 15, Funding; Declaration of competing interest

eligibility.reason: Randomised crossover: students were randomly divided into two groups that did one task with ChatGPT and one without, in counterbalanced order (p. 4, Section 3.2.1; Fig. 1 p. 5). 51 people analyzed (Group A 24, Group B 27; Tables 3-5), just above the 50 threshold; no exclusions reported. The first-period (Task 1) between-group contrast also uses all 51. Outcomes are scored on the ideas: researcher-coded counts of ideas, categories, unique and existing solutions, word counts, drawing codes, and LaBSE embedding distances (Table 2, p. 7; p. 7).

one_line_finding: Within person, ChatGPT left fluency, flexibility, and originality unchanged (Table 4, p. 8) but raised the count of ideas resembling existing products (0.55 to 1.00, p = .011) and cut description length (25.57 to 23.36 words, p = .015); students who used AI first scored higher on flexibility and originality in their later unaided task (interaction p = .001 and p < .001, p. 8; Table 5, p. 9).
open_questions: Semantic divergence direction: printed means are 0.28 unaided vs 0.29 AI-assisted at both group and individual level, d = -0.26 and d = 0.48, and Fig. 3 shows higher divergence for AI-assisted ideas, yet the abstract and text (p. 1, p. 10, p. 13) say divergence was lower with AI (homogenisation). The form codes direction from the printed numbers; the extraction phase should resolve which is right.

Individual-level semantic divergence uses a paired t-test with df = 364, which does not match 51 participants (expected df = 50); the methods describe pairwise divergence within each participant but the results describe divergence from the centroid per participant (p. 7 vs p. 10).
Group-level t-test reports df = 728, equal to the total number of ideas rather than N - 2.

Whether n_randomized = 51 should be recorded: the paper gives 51 participants randomly divided into groups of 24 and 27 (Fig. 1) and reports no exclusions, but does not separately state counts at assignment.

The after_ai contrasts (S1-O12 to S1-O15) compare Group B's unaided Task 2 with Group A's unaided Task 1: different tasks and later in the session, so prior AI exposure is confounded with task and practice. The paper tests the order effect only through the mixed ANOVA interaction.
notes: Single study with participant-level outcomes. Table 4 pools both tasks (N = 102 person-condition observations; Wilcoxon signed-rank). Table 5 gives Mann-Whitney tests by task; the Task 1 contrast is a clean between-subjects comparison with no prior exposure. Task 2 AI vs unaided contrasts are recorded but their control arm had used AI in Task 1. Omitted from the outcome list (15-outcome cap): after_ai versions of text elaboration (Group B Task 2 unaided 25.60 (7.39) vs Group A Task 1 unaided 25.54 (8.92)) and image elaboration (1.29 (0.36) vs 1.35 (0.35)), both in Table 5 p. 9. Not outcomes: baseline balance (Table 3, p. 7: prior assignments A1-A5 and GPA, all p > .24), prompt statistics (Table 8, 341 prompts in 49 conversations) and interaction codes (Table 9). Ideas per cell: Group A T1 unaided 158, Group B T1 AI 195, Group B T2 unaided 202, Group A T2 AI 173 (Fig. 1, p. 5). The novelty and originality codes were assigned by the researchers through consensus without reported inter-rater agreement (p. 5).
